query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the in-flight particle velocity during HVAF-i7 spraying by adjusting torch gas flow and optimizing the spray distance to around 300–350 mm will improve deposition efficiency so that FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy coatings achieve a sufficient thickness while preserving acceptable oxidation and adhesion characteristics.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas-atomized FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a particle size of 15–45 μm, as used in earlier HVAF-M3 coatings.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 torch parameters to increase particle velocity – for example, by increasing the gas (oxygen/fuel) flow rates and setting the spray distance to the nozzle-specific optimum (300–350 mm).
generation.conditions: Deposition on substrates (including internal diameters as small as 120 mm) under standard HVAF-i7 operational settings with service-level high-temperature thermal–barrier conditions; ensuring that the substrate temperature and ambient oxygen levels mimic those in the target application.
generation.structural_mediator: Higher particle kinetic energy results in improved impact, flattening, and interfacial bonding of the feedstock particles, which facilitates a denser, thicker coating buildup.
generation.mechanism: By increasing particle velocity, the feedstock particles gain more kinetic energy, leading to better substrate impingement and reduced in-flight deceleration. This reduces premature cooling and oxidation while enhancing deposition efficiency so that a thicker, adherent coating forms with controlled oxide formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline HVAF-i7 process with standard parameters (which produces acceptable quality but inadequate thickness), the intervention is expected to yield coatings with significantly increased thickness while maintaining coating integrity, low as-sprayed oxidation, and durability for high-temperature thermal-barrier service.
generation.baseline: FeCoNiCrAl HEA coatings produced using the HVAF-i7 torch with the same 15–45 μm feedstock but without additional adjustments to particle velocity, resulting in acceptable quality but insufficient overall thickness.
generation.boundary: This intervention should remain effective as long as the adjusted parameters do not induce excessive oxidation or compromise phase composition; the benefits are expected under operational conditions mimicking those used in conventional MCrAlY bond coat studies (e.g., nozzle distances around 300–350 mm) and for substrates with internal diameters down to 120 mm. Extreme changes in gas chemistry or spray distance beyond the tested range may lead to other undesirable effects.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in coating thickness and the precise balance between increased deposition efficiency and oxidation control are uncertain until experimentally verified. There is also uncertainty about whether the optimal spray distances determined for MCrAlY coatings translate directly to the HVAF-i7 process for HEAs.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled study using the HVAF-i7 torch with FeCoNiCrAl HEA powder (15–45 μm). Prepare two sets of samples: one set using the standard HVAF-i7 parameters (serving as the control) and another set using the adjusted parameters (increased gas flow rate and a spray distance of 300–350 mm) intended to raise particle velocity. For both sets, deposit coatings on substrates with internal diameters as small as 120 mm under identical ambient and preheat conditions.
measurements: Coating thickness measured by cross-sectional microscopy
In-flight particle velocity (using diagnostic tools if available)
Oxide content and phase composition by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings produced using the increased particle velocity and optimized spray distance do not show a statistically significant increase in thickness compared to the control (without sacrificing the acceptable oxidation and adhesion levels), or if they exhibit compromised microstructural properties or excessive oxidation, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As reported in [,,,], HVOF as-sprayed AlTiCrFeCoNi coatings possessed a dense microstructure and a high microhardness over 750 HV with a good fracture toughness. The heat-treated NiCoFeCrSiAlTi coating exhibits a hardness even higher than 800 HV, good wear resistance, and oxidation resistance at 1100 °C, similar to that of MCrAlY coating []. The cavitation erosion resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi coating is about 3.5 times that of 06Cr13Ni5Mo steel in the same environment []. The high wear resistance of AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA at elevated temperatures is associated with oxidation behavior. The formation of a compact oxide layer on the AlCoCrFeNi and AlTiCrFeCoNi HVOF coatings accounts for enhanced wear resistance at temperatures ≥ 800 °C [] and a lowered coefficient of friction due to its function as a solid lubricant []. In [], it was found that additions of Nd and Mo to a AlCrFeCoNi base significantly reduced the wear depth at increasing temperatures due to improved oxide layer adhesion. Thus, AlCoCrFeNiMo coatings deposited using HVOF are suitable for high-temperature application. A unique feature of thermal spray processes is the extremely high heating and cooling rates (>106 K/s) [,,

Therefore, as-sprayed HEA coatings may possess different phase constitution compared with their as-cast counterparts [] as well as with the feedstock powder [,]. For example, both as-cast AlSiTiCrFeCoNiMo0.5 and AlSiTiCrFeNiMo0.5 are dual-phase alloys (BCC + FCC); however, if fabricated via thermal spray, they have only the supersaturated BCC solid solution []. Cold-sprayed AlFeNiCoCr alloy retains the same BCC structure as was observed in the powder []. In contrast, in the plasma-sprayed coating of the same composition, the FCC phase is observed as the major one []. Despite high heating and cooling rates, which prevent the elements’ diffusion development, factors such as high temperature, high oxygen concentration, and high specific surface of the powder inevitably lead to in-flight oxidation. The existence of oxides in the flame-sprayed HEA coatings due to in-flight oxidation improves the hardness and wear of the coatings compared to those of cold-sprayed ones [].
